name: Farside
label: Revelation
lede: Farside came out of Orange County with Zack de la Rocha on second guitar, passed on the major labels when punk went gold in 1994, and broke up after three albums on Revelation.

eras.title: Straight edge, borrowed gear, and Zack on guitar
eras.text: Farside grew out of the late-'80s Orange County straight edge scene, in the same crowd as Inside Out and Sense Field. For a stretch their second guitarist was Zack de la Rocha of University High, who left before the first album and went on to Rage Against the Machine.

years.cap: Popeye Vogelsang singing at Farside's first show of the 1992 tour, Salt Lake City, June 1992
years.h: Popeye Vogelsang asks for a tryout and ends up singing
years.p: Guitarist Rob Haworth, bassist Josh Stanton and drummer Bob Beshear already had a band. Michael "Popeye" Vogelsang asked to try out and became the singer and a guitarist.

yt: Full set, Miramar Theatre, San Clemente, May 25, 1990
years.h: Zack de la Rocha plays second guitar in Farside
years.p: Zack de la Rocha, also singing in [[Inside Out|0049c4d7-6459-4b54-a865-fd19969f427f]], plays second lead guitar in Farside in 1990–91. He never makes a Farside album, but he is on the early demos later collected on Scrap.
years.xp:
De la Rocha went to University High in Irvine, the same school scene Farside came from. By late 1991 he was fronting Rage Against the Machine.

Popeye told OC Weekly in 1999: "It was an enjoyable experience when Zack was in the band. He's a great guy, a very talented guitar player."

years.h: Rochambeau is cut on Christmas Day with borrowed gear
years.p: Farside's Revelation debut was recorded at For The Record Studios with equipment lent by friends. Popeye wrote just one of its songs, Worlds; Trouser Press heard acoustic guitars and songs about unity and the personal as political.

eras.title: Louder, thicker, and not for sale
eras.text: With Kevin Murphy writing alongside Popeye, Farside got heavier. Then the Offspring and Green Day turned Southern California punk into a gold rush, and Farside said no to the people holding the checkbooks.

years.cap: Farside live in Morgantown, West Virginia, June 1992
years.h: Touring fill-in Kevin Murphy takes Rob Haworth's spot
years.p: Kevin Murphy plays guitar on tour, then joins Farside full time in 1993, replacing Haworth. From here Murphy and Popeye Vogelsang write the songs together.

years.h: Rigged, the second album fans still rank first
years.p: Producer Jim Monroe pushes Farside louder and thicker. Popeye says the title came from gear held together with bubblegum and rubber bands.
years.xp: The line-up is Popeye Vogelsang, Kevin Murphy, bassist Bryan Chu and drummer Bob Beshear. Trouser Press heard twin guitars that gnarl forcefully and melodies with a Hüsker Dü streak, from the punk rush of Square One to a melancholy closer.

years.big: We have total creative control and can do whatever the fuck we want to.
yt: How Farside became a Revelation band, Aftermath #17
years.h: Majors come calling in 1994, and Farside stay on Revelation
years.p: Popeye Vogelsang's answer, as OC Weekly printed it, when the 1994 punk boom sent labels through Orange County. Farside passed on the major-label offers and stayed with Huntington Beach's Revelation Records.
years.xp:
The members went to college and built careers instead. By 1999 Popeye was editing an employee newsletter in Los Angeles by day.

He told OC Weekly: "We were happy with what we had and still have with Revelation Records."

years.h: Scrap collects the early demos, with Zack de la Rocha on second guitar
years.p: A compilation of Farside's early recordings, including demos from the line-up with De la Rocha on second guitar.

years.h: Six weeks across Europe, booked three weeks before the van left
years.p: Behind Rigged, Farside take a rented van around Europe. It was the band's last real tour for four years.
years.xp:
Popeye told Dying Scene the six-week tour came together roughly three weeks before they were due to leave, and that it was one mishap after another: Murphy hit a new BMW in Paris, and the van skidded on snowy roads in Italy.

He still called it "one of the most incredible adventures of my life."

years.h: The self-titled EP is a bridge to the last album
years.p: Six songs on Revelation. Popeye has said it wasn't anyone's favorite Farside release.
years.xp: Popeye told Dying Scene the band had a few new songs and figured, why not record them. He said the EP never fully hung together, though some listeners liked the acoustic songs and the cover photo.

eras.title: A farewell record, over budget
eras.text: Farside went quiet for years while the members built lives. They came back for one more record, knowing it would be their last, and spent more than they had making it.

years.h: The Monroe Doctrine takes its name from engineer Jim Monroe
years.p: Farside's third album, made as a farewell and over budget. OC Weekly counted acoustic ballads, grindcore, speed-metal riffs and a cover of Graham Parker's Blue Highway.
years.xp: Popeye told Dying Scene the process was long and tenuous, and that treating it as their last record made the band willing to take risks. The title credits Monroe, who engineered the sessions.

years.h: Bassist Bryan Chu trades the stage for a kindergarten classroom
years.p: Bryan Chu marries and moves to San Francisco to teach kindergarten, OC Weekly reported. Sean "Rosey" Rosenthal, 21, takes over on bass.

years.h: A summer on the East Coast with Fastbreak and Save the Day
years.p: Farside's first tour since 1995 runs up the East Coast with Fastbreak and Save the Day.
years.xp: Popeye told OC Weekly: "We had a good time and even turned a profit, which was nice."

years.h: Live at the Melody Bar, New Brunswick NJ, August 3, 1999
yt: Live at the Melody Bar, New Brunswick NJ, August 3, 1999

years.h: Eleven years in, Farside split after a last tour
years.p: After three albums and two EPs, Farside call it after one last tour. Popeye has said the breakup was mutual.
years.xp: Popeye told Dying Scene the members were "all getting older and moving in different directions." Nobody fought; the band simply ran its course.

eras.title: The songs outlast the band
eras.text: Farside never played again, and Popeye has said he has no interest in trying. The songs kept turning up anyway: in a snowboarding game, on anniversary vinyl, and in a new Popeye band back on Revelation.

years.h: A snowboarding game picks up Seven Day Constant
years.p: Farside's Seven Day Constant lands on the soundtrack of Amped: Freestyle Snowboarding. Popeye starts Your Favorite Trainwreck with [[Jeff Caudill|6a41fff4-9b5c-4b1c-9ebf-4df434fdbbec]] of [[Gameface|c67fddd4-970b-4bfb-8996-314c29b08f27]].

years.h: Popeye gets paid to goof off in front of a microphone
years.p: Three years into professional voice-over work for animation, commercials and video games, Popeye Vogelsang told Dying Scene that was the job in a sentence.

q: I've always been super proud of Farside's tenure with Revelation.
years.h: Popeye's new band [[Calling Hours|a76e3280-2524-461d-855f-0550ebedff93]] puts out Say Less on Revelation
years.p: Popeye Vogelsang sings over four members of [[Don't Sleep|0f073ffb-b2de-4017-9646-bf80a73079ec]]; [[Brian McTernan|eda2cb2f-b2c6-4e74-9fd7-49ea52df4172]] of [[Battery|172d89ba-95ab-4e30-92a2-fe836ba0601e]] produces. McTernan and Judge's [[Sammy Siegler|869c662b-574c-46ac-acf6-3dc6f025fd5a]] steered the demos to Jordan Cooper.

years.h: Thirty years on, Rigged comes back on mint green vinyl
years.p: Revelation reissues Rigged on mint green eco-vinyl with a 16-page booklet, plus new color pressings of Rochambeau and The Monroe Doctrine. Still no reunion shows.
